input_signals.name: loss_firm_external_finance_dependence
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross external financing raised by firms with persistently negative earnings reflects a funding gap being plugged rather than growth capital, and such firms subsequently underperform as dilution, covenant pressure, and refinancing risk resolve badly.
input_signals.reasoning: The indicator turns the signal on only for firms whose three-year average ROA is negative, making the interaction explicitly state-contingent rather than a rescaled financing variable. Combining debt and equity inflows captures total dependence on outside capital, which is benign for profitable firms but predictive of poor returns for chronic losers.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( winsor( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), at ), 1 ) ), indicator( neg( ma( ratio( ib, at ), 3 ) ), 0 ) )

input_signals.name: borrowing_without_tax_shield
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1)), RANK(NEG(SUMRANK(RATIO(txt, at), RATIO(pi, lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Debt is cheap only when its interest is deductible; a firm paying negligible taxes with weak pretax income earns no tax shield from incremental borrowing, so net new debt in that state is pure risk-shifting and predicts low returns, whereas the same borrowing by a taxpaying firm has an offsetting benefit.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the mis-scaled payout-over-book-equity construct entirely and introduces tax-shield exhaustion — built from txt and pi, essentially unused in the archive — as the conditioning state, so it does not recycle retained-earnings or leverage-change information. Paired with the accepted deep-leverage gate on the same net-borrowing flow, it isolates *which* distress dimension makes borrowing harmful: proximity to the default boundary or absence of any tax benefit.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( dltis, dltr ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( sumrank( ratio( txt, at ), ratio( pi, lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: borrowing_into_working_capital_drain
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at))), RANK(SUMRANK(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, at), 1), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: When a firm's cash becomes trapped in growing receivables and inventory while operations generate little cash, new borrowing funds an operating deterioration rather than investment; such debt-financed working-capital expansion signals unsold output and weakening collections, and predicts low returns.
input_signals.reasoning: The distress state here is a working-capital *drain* combined with weak cash generation, a channel the archive has never tested — previous distress legs used leverage, retained earnings, cash buffers, taxes or sales growth. It also differentiates from Signal 5 by conditioning identical net borrowing on an operating-liquidity deterioration rather than on tax-shield exhaustion, so the pair identifies which state makes incremental debt harmful.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( rank( ratio( sub( dltis, dltr ), at ) ) ), rank( sumrank( delta( ratio( wcap, at ), 1 ), neg( ratio( oancf, lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: internal_vs_external_wall_coverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(oancf, che), lct), 1)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), lct), 1))), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(ib, lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Two firms can cover the same near-term claims from very different sources; a levered, weak-earnings firm whose current liabilities are covered by internal cash generation and cash on hand is self-sustaining, while one whose coverage comes from freshly raised outside money is dependent on continued market access and is riskier than its coverage ratio suggests.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the equity-versus-debt mix question — which the archive has now tested twice with results opposite to a positive sign — and replaces it with the untested question of whether near-term claim coverage is internally or externally sourced, which no single-theme sort computes. The mean-zero difference of bounded ranks prevents the cash-flow leg from dominating the variance and keeps both tails populated by levered weak-earnings firms, so the spread is a coverage-source contrast rather than a profitability sort.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( winsor( ratio( add( oancf, che ), lct ), 1 ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), lct ), 1 ) ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( lt, at ), neg( ratio( ib, lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: liquidity_built_without_leverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(che, lct), 1), 1)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ib, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Where a weak firm's liquidity came from determines what it means: a rising cash-to-current-liabilities buffer achieved without net new borrowing reflects internally generated slack and predicts higher returns, whereas an unchanged or falling buffer alongside net borrowing means the new debt was consumed and the firm is worse off than its leverage alone implies.
input_signals.reasoning: This drops the tax-shield construction entirely, so it is not a re-scaled re-test, and instead asks whether liquidity improvements are self-financed or debt-financed — the "borrow and hoard versus borrow and burn" question that gen-1 probed with a contaminated non-negative rank product and therefore never actually answered. Both legs are bounded ranks combined as a mean-zero difference, which is the structure that has produced consistent portfolio and cross-sectional evidence in this archive, and the weak-earnings weight makes the distinction economically binding.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( winsor( delta( ratio( che, lct ), 1 ), 1 ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( sub( dltis, dltr ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), 1 ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( ib, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: industry_relative_external_dependence
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), lct), 1)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(ib, lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: External funding dependence is only informative relative to the industry's normal funding pattern: biotechnology and utilities raise outside capital as a matter of course, so a firm's dependence should be judged against its peers, and firms unusually dependent on outside money relative to their industry underperform.
input_signals.reasoning: The raw version of this leg produced the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope (t = −5.24) yet no portfolio alpha, a pattern that points to industry composition dominating the extreme deciles — the short tail fills with structurally issuance-heavy industries whose returns FF5 factors already span. Industry demeaning, a treatment the archive has never used, targets exactly that failure and would convert cross-sectional content into a tradable spread if the diagnosis is right.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), lct ), 1 ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( lt, at ), neg( ratio( ib, lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: funding_source_contrast_in_wc_deficit
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(oancf, che), lct), 1)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), lct), 1))), INDICATOR(RATIO(lct, act), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: The identity of the money paying near-term claims matters most where the balance sheet cannot cover them: for firms whose current liabilities exceed current assets, internal versus external coverage is the difference between survival and dependence on continued market access, while for firms with comfortable working capital it is a matter of indifference.
input_signals.reasoning: This tests whether the double-strong result is a threshold phenomenon concentrated in genuine working-capital deficit rather than a smooth function of leverage and earnings, using an economically canonical cutoff (current ratio below one) instead of an arbitrary numeric threshold. Because the financing leg is a mean-zero rank difference, the excluded firms sit at zero in the interior deciles while both extreme deciles contain working-capital-deficit firms with opposite funding sources, preserving a clean interaction spread.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( winsor( ratio( add( oancf, che ), lct ), 1 ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), lct ), 1 ) ) ), indicator( ratio( lct, act ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: earnings_based_wall_coverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(che, ib), lct), 1)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), lct), 1))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: If the funding-source effect is about genuine cash available to creditors, replacing operating cash flow with accounting earnings in the internal leg should weaken it; if the effect is instead about a broader notion of solvency that the market underprices, the earnings-based version should work as well or better.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a substantive test of what the internal resource is — cash generation versus accrual earnings — a question that separates a liquidity mechanism from a profitability mechanism, and the critic has repeatedly warned that oancf-based legs risk being cash-flow-anomaly rediscoveries. The distress weight is trimmed to leverage alone so that ib does not appear on both sides of the expression, and dropping oancf should also lift coverage from roughly 0.076 toward 0.11.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( winsor( ratio( add( che, ib ), lct ), 1 ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), lct ), 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: raising_against_a_debt_heavy_wall
input_signals.hypothesis: Outside capital raised when a firm's near-term claims are dominated by financial debt rather than trade payables is money raised to satisfy creditors on a fixed schedule, a forced transaction; the same raising by a firm whose current claims are mostly operating payables is discretionary and far less ominous.
input_signals.reasoning: This asks a new question about the external leg that carries the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope: whether the *composition* of the claims being funded determines when issuance is toxic, which is different from conditioning on leverage, earnings or cash. Because the composition weight is a bounded, non-negative rank and the financing leg is centred, the tails contrast forced raisers against firms raising against payables-dominated claims, and a portfolio alpha here would explain why the raw external leg has slope but no spread.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( rank( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), lct ) ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, lct ) ) )

input_signals.name: coverage_decay_replaced_by_issuance
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(oancf, che), lct), 1), 1)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), lct), 1))), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(ib, lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is the direction in which a firm's funding is migrating: a levered, weak-earnings firm whose internal coverage of current claims is deteriorating while it leans on fresh outside money is substituting market access for self-sufficiency, and that substitution predicts low returns even when the current coverage level still looks adequate.
input_signals.reasoning: This is not a denominator swap on the archive signal but a change-versus-level contrast: the internal leg becomes the one-year change in coverage while the external leg stays a level, so the signal identifies firms whose funding composition is shifting rather than firms that are statically self-sufficient. Because coverage levels are highly persistent and issuance is lumpy, the substitution dynamic is close to orthogonal to the level contrast already evaluated, and it makes a genuinely new prediction about the timing of the mispricing.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( winsor( delta( ratio( add( oancf, che ), lct ), 1 ), 1 ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), lct ), 1 ) ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( lt, at ), neg( ratio( ib, lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: capital_raised_per_unit_of_revenue
input_signals.hypothesis: Scaling outside capital by revenue measures how many months of business activity the firm had to finance externally; when current claims are also large relative to revenue, the operating base is too small to retire those claims and the firm must keep returning to markets, predicting low returns.
input_signals.reasoning: Every previous version of the external-dependence leg was scaled by balance-sheet claims or assets, so revenue — the flow that ultimately extinguishes obligations — is an untested and economically natural yardstick that behaves very differently for asset-light and inventory-heavy firms. The conditioning variable, claims per unit of revenue, is likewise a new distress dimension in this archive and gives the interaction a clear meaning: external funding is dangerous exactly when the revenue base cannot service the claim stock.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( rank( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), sale ) ) ), rank( ratio( lct, sale ) ) )

input_signals.name: self_sufficiency_conjunction
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(MIN(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(oancf, che), lct), 1)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), lct), 1))))), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(ib, lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: True self-sufficiency requires both conditions at once — internal resources that cover near-term claims *and* an absence of reliance on outside money — and firms satisfying both should outperform, whereas a firm strong on one dimension and weak on the other is not protected.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has only tested this mechanism as a difference, which lets a very high internal coverage rank offset heavy issuance and vice versa; the conjunction asks whether the economics are really a logical AND, a distinct functional claim rather than an ablation of the conditioning. Cross-sectionally demeaning the MIN before applying the distress weight avoids the failure mode diagnosed in generation 3, where non-negative rank products turned the sort into a distress-level bet.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( min( rank( winsor( ratio( add( oancf, che ), lct ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), lct ), 1 ) ) ) ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( lt, at ), neg( ratio( ib, lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: frequency_of_market_dependence
input_signals.hypothesis: Chronic dependence is better measured by how often a firm must return to capital markets than by how much it raised in any one year; a firm that has made a material capital raise in each of the last three years while its internal resources fail to cover current claims is structurally reliant on outside money and underperforms.
input_signals.reasoning: Every dependence measure in the archive is a magnitude, so frequency is a genuinely new dimension, and it is economically distinct: one large raise can fund years of operations, whereas repeated raises reveal that each infusion is consumed before the next. Counting years above a 5%-of-assets materiality threshold also removes the scale skewness that has repeatedly split this archive's FMB and portfolio evidence, since the resulting variable takes only four values and cannot be dominated by tail observations.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ts_sum( indicator( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), at ), 0.05 ), 3 ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( che, oancf ), lct ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: internal_generation_vs_consumed_capital
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(oancf, lct), 1)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltis, sstk), DELTA(che, 1)), lct), 1))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital raised and still sitting on the balance sheet as cash is not a warning sign; capital raised and already gone — consumed by operations or obligations within the same year — is. Netting the cash build out of gross inflows isolates consumed external capital, and levered firms that generate cash internally rather than consuming outside money should outperform.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces a discretised re-test of the dependence leg with a new financing object built from the cash-flow identity: inflows minus the change in cash equals what was absorbed, which distinguishes funded-and-hoarding firms from funded-and-burning firms — the distinction gen-1 attempted with a non-negative rank product that turned into a distress-level sort. It keeps the difference-of-bounded-ranks structure that has produced both cross-sectional and portfolio evidence in this archive, with internal cash generation as the opposing leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( winsor( ratio( oancf, lct ), 1 ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( sub( add( dltis, sstk ), delta( che, 1 ) ), lct ), 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: working_capital_buffer_vs_dependence
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(wcap, lct), 1)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), lct), 1))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Creditors can be paid not only from cash but from the whole net working-capital buffer — receivables collected and inventory sold within the year; the economically correct internal resource is therefore net working capital relative to current claims, and levered firms with a thick buffer and little market reliance should outperform.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than splicing two proxies across reporting eras, this states a single, uniform economic claim about which resources are available to extinguish near-term claims, and it is a different claim from the cash-and-cash-flow versions because receivables and inventory are convertible but not liquid. Because wcap is a balance-sheet item reported throughout the sample, coverage should rise from roughly 0.076 to above 0.11 without any change in the population's proxy definition over time.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( winsor( ratio( wcap, lct ), 1 ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), lct ), 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: weakest_link_funding_vulnerability
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(MAX(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), lct), 1)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(che, oancf), lct), 1))))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm is vulnerable if *either* of its funding pillars fails — thin internal coverage of near-term claims or heavy reliance on outside money — so the binding constraint is the worse of the two dimensions, and levered firms scoring high on that maximum should underperform.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has tested this mechanism as a difference (trade-off) and as a MIN conjunction (both-must-hold on the safe side) but never as a maximum, which is a distinct functional claim: vulnerability is determined by the worst pillar, not by the average or by the safest one. This is not another centred-dependence-times-weight construction, because the financing and distress quantities are combined non-linearly before centring, so the tails contain firms failing on different dimensions.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( max( rank( winsor( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), lct ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( ratio( add( che, oancf ), lct ), 1 ) ) ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: revenue_coverage_vs_dependence
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(sale, lct), 1)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), lct), 1))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Near-term claims are ultimately extinguished by the operating cycle, so revenue relative to current liabilities measures how many times a year the business turns over its claims; a levered firm with high claim turnover can meet obligations from operations, while one with slow turnover and heavy reliance on raised capital cannot.
input_signals.reasoning: This substitutes an operating-flow measure of claim-servicing capacity for the stock-and-cash-flow measures tested so far, which is a different economic statement — throughput rather than liquidity — and it avoids the equity-identity constructions the critic identified as known anomalies. Sales are reported universally, so like Signal 2 it materially raises coverage while keeping the difference-of-ranks structure that has generated the archive's only doubly significant results.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( winsor( ratio( sale, lct ), 1 ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), lct ), 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: weakest_link_with_buffer
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(MAX(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), lct), 1)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(wcap, lct), 1))))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A levered firm is vulnerable if either its liquid buffer is thin or its reliance on raised capital is heavy, and the binding constraint is whichever is worse; using the net working-capital buffer as the liquidity pillar should sharpen this weakest-link measure relative to a cash-and-cash-flow pillar.
input_signals.reasoning: The MAX form produced the archive's cleanest short-side result (alpha −3.5%, t = −2.50, Sharpe −0.38) with the cash-based pillar, while the buffer-based resource proved the stronger pillar in the difference form with 45% more coverage, so this asks whether the two findings compound. It is a substantive test of which liquidity pillar binds rather than a rescaling, and its answer determines which construction the final generation should consolidate on the short side.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( max( rank( winsor( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), lct ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( ratio( wcap, lct ), 1 ) ) ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: funding_contrast_under_claim_urgency
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(wcap, lct), 1)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltis, sstk), lct), 1))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Funding self-sufficiency matters in proportion to how soon obligations fall due: a firm whose liabilities are mostly long-dated has time to repair itself, while one with a large share of its total liabilities in current debt must meet claims now, making the internal-versus-external contrast immediately binding.
input_signals.reasoning: Every version of this contrast has been weighted by leverage *level* or earnings weakness, but the mechanism is about timing, so the economically appropriate conditioning variable is the share of total liabilities that is short-dated — an urgency dimension the archive has used only once, on the dependence leg alone. If urgency is the right weight, both metrics should improve on the leverage-weighted benchmark without any change to the informative legs.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( winsor( ratio( wcap, lct ), 1 ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( add( dltis, sstk ), lct ), 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, lt ) ) )
